q1.directions: Use the passage below to answer all parts of the question that follows.

parts.a: Describe ONE outcome of the Opium Wars for China.
parts.b: Explain ONE cause of Britain's decision to go to war in 1839.
parts.c: Explain ONE difference between the Opium Wars and the Scramble for Africa as forms of imperialism.

sample_answers.a: China was forced to open treaty ports to foreign trade, cede Hong Kong to Britain, and grant foreigners extraterritoriality — exemption from Chinese law.
sample_answers.b: One cause was the trade imbalance: Britain's appetite for tea created a silver drain that opium sales reversed, and when Lin destroyed the opium, British merchants and the government chose war to protect the profitable trade.
sample_answers.c: In China, Britain imposed unequal treaties and spheres of influence without formal colonization, while in Africa Europeans partitioned the continent into directly ruled colonies — informal empire versus formal empire.

q1.stimulus: The Opium Wars began as a trade dispute and ended as a demonstration. Britain sold opium grown in India to China to balance the tea trade; when Commissioner Lin Zexu seized and destroyed the drug in 1839, Britain sent gunboats. The Treaties of Nanjing (1842) and Tianjin (1858) opened ports, ceded Hong Kong, and imposed extraterritoriality. For China it was the start of the 'century of humiliation'; for Britain it was proof that industrial military power could force open any market.

q2.attribution: —Adapted from Commissioner Lin Zexu, letter to Queen Victoria, 1839
q2.directions: Use the passage below to answer all parts of the question that follows.

parts.a: Identify ONE argument Lin makes in the passage.
parts.b: Explain ONE way the passage reflects the Qing government's view of the opium trade.
parts.c: Explain ONE reason Lin's moral argument failed to prevent war.

sample_answers.a: Lin argues that Britain's own ban on opium proves it knows the drug is harmful, making it hypocritical to profit from selling it in China.
sample_answers.b: The passage reflects the Qing view that opium was a moral poison destroying Chinese society and draining its silver — a legitimate target of state prohibition, like any contraband.
sample_answers.c: His argument failed because Britain's decision was driven by commercial and strategic interests, not moral consistency: the British government backed its merchants with gunboats regardless of the hypocrisy Lin exposed.

q2.stimulus: We have heard that in your own country opium is prohibited with the utmost strictness and severity. This is a strong proof that you know how hurtful it is to mankind. How can you then sell it in China and profit from poisoning our people?

q3.attribution: Painting of the Thirteen Factories at Canton (Guangzhou), c. 1820
q3.directions: Use the image below to answer all parts of the question that follows.

parts.a: Describe ONE feature of the factories shown in the image.
parts.b: Explain ONE way the Canton system restricted foreign trade before 1842.
parts.c: Explain ONE change the Treaty of Nanjing brought to the system shown in the image.

sample_answers.a: The image shows a row of Western-style warehouses and offices flying foreign flags, confined within a walled compound on the riverfront — visibly segregated from the Chinese city.
sample_answers.b: All foreign merchants were confined to this single compound, could trade only through licensed Chinese hong merchants, and could not enter China proper — the Qing controlled every aspect of the exchange.
sample_answers.c: The treaty abolished the monopoly system: Britain gained the right to trade at five ports instead of one, and British merchants no longer had to go through the hong — the confinement shown in the image ended.

q3.stimulus: Painting of the Thirteen Factories at Canton (Guangzhou) circa 1820: the walled compound of foreign trading houses flying European and American flags, where all legal Western trade with China was confined before the Opium Wars.
